newsitem.title: USA: Mystery cash in Texas may indicate money laundering.
newsitem.headline: Mystery cash in Texas may indicate money laundering.

text.p: A mysterious $3 billion cash surplus at a Texas branch of the Federal Reserve may indicate illicit money laundering activity in the area, former law enforcement officials warned Congress Thursday.

The surplus at the San Antonio Branch of the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas "is indeed indicative somewhat of narcotics money laundering occuring there and in Mexico," Charles Saphos, former head of the Justice Department's narcotics division, said at a Congressional hearing here.
Saphos, who also was a U.S. Attorney in southern Florida and general counsel for Interpol, disputed earlier testimony by Clinton administration officials that the surplus was meaningless.
"It is such a serious symptom that it should not be ignored by any professional," Saphos told the House Banking Committee.

Federal Reserve banks collect and distribute cash to commercial banks around the country to meet daily business needs. A surplus occurs when a branch takes in more cash from surrounding banks than it sends back to the Fed.

Earlier at the hearing, Stanley Morris, director of the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network known as FinCEN, dismissed the surplus in San Antonio and a few other Fed branches as irrelevent.
"We can now say definitively that cash surpluses at the Federal Reserve banks are not indicators of money laundering," Morris said.
In San Antonio, the surplus is largely a result of legitimate transfers of excess cash from Mexican banks to U.S. banks in Texas, according to a study by the Internal Revenue Service cited by Morris.
The U.S. banks then transfer the cash to the Fed branch, where it is no longer meaningful to law enforcement officials, Morris explained.

While tracking the proceeds of crime is critical, once the money enters the banking system "the cash transaction, the currency itself, is no longer the proceeds of crime," Morris said. "It's essentially been layered into the system so that the cash is no longer a matter of law enforcement interest."
And while San Antonio showed a surplus, the Federal Reserve in New York City, a hotbed of drug money laundering, reported a $28 billion deficit, Morris pointed out.

Representative Henry Gonzalez, Democrat of Texas, charged in January that the San Antonio surplus could be the result of money laundering by Mexican drug dealers and called for Congressional hearings.

"According to FinCEN, the cash surpluses may not be, in and of themselves, money laundering," Gonzalez said at Thursday's hearing. "But these surpluses tell you that a great deal of unexplained cash is moving through a particular area."
